conflict_topics: who cooks / separate pots / extra work
dialogue_quality_notes: Conversation is concise and goal-oriented: participants identify constraints, propose options, and test acceptability.
Agent A emphasizes the norm of a shared meal; Agents B and C respond pragmatically (e.g. 'As long as we all eat at 6.30, it works for me').
Agent D offers both accommodation (vegetarian night for all) and practical help (recipes), helping to resolve the issue.
evaluation.final_reason: Agent D proposed a mixed arrangement and everyone accepted: D offered 'How about on my night, I cook a vegetarian meal for everyone?... On the other nights, I'd still have to make my own' (Round 4). The group later accepted the practical solution: 'Okay, that's fine. It's probably easiest for everyone if I just make my own food on your nights.' (Agent D, Round 10) and Agent A responded, 'Okay. If that's what everyone wants.' (Agent A, Round 10). Thus D agreed to cook vegetarian for all on his night and to prepare his own separate food on others' nights; the others accepted that arrangement.
position_change_notes: Agent D: moved from requesting an accommodation to proposing a concrete mixed solution (vegetarian night for all; cook own on other nights) and then accepted the final arrangement. Evidence: Round 4 offer and Round 10 acceptance.

Agent A: initially resisted losing the shared-meal norm ('the whole point was for us to eat the same meal together') but accepted the group's practical choice: 'Okay. If that's what everyone wants.' (Round 10).
Agent C: initially refused extra cooking ('I'm not cooking two separate meals') and later supported the low-burden solution ('I agree with Agent B. That sounds like the easiest way').
Agent B: remained pragmatic throughout and supported the solution early ('As long as we all eat at 6.30, it works for me').

round_scores.evidence: Agent D introduces a new constraint: 'I'll be vegetarian for the whole month - no meat, fish, or eggs. And I can't eat from pots that have cooked meat in them during that time.' This creates a potential incompatibility with the existing shared-meal rota though no one objects yet.

Agents start to surface the practical implications: 'So we'd need separate pots for your food?' and 'Does that mean cooking two separate meals? I have to eat at 6.30 for my shift.' This shows a clearer logistical disagreement and time constraint.

Agent C explicitly refuses extra work: 'Yeah, I'm not cooking two separate meals on my night.' Agent D offers an alternative: 'I can just cook something vegetarian for myself. I can use my own pot.' The refusal is a clear disagreement but D's proposal reduces the burden on others.

Agent A objects to losing the shared-meal aspect: 'But if you're cooking your own thing, then we're not really sharing a meal, are we?' Agent D proposes a compromise for his night: 'How about on my night, I cook a vegetarian meal for everyone?... On the other nights, I'd still have to make my own.' The disagreement about other nights remains.

Agent A points out the remaining issue: 'Okay, but that only fixes one night. The other three nights we're still not really eating together, are we?' Agent B is unconcerned about that aspect, showing persistent disagreement.

Agent D acknowledges the limitation ('I know it's not the same on the other nights...') while Agent A reiterates the core value: 'the whole point was for us to eat the same meal together.' The substantive incompatibility remains unresolved.

Agent D presses for a solution ('But given I can't eat what you're cooking, what do you suggest we do instead?' and 'So we need a solution. Do you have one?'). There is still no agreement on how to reconcile shared meals with D's restriction.

Agent A says they 'don't really know how to cook vegetarian dishes.' Agent D offers practical help: 'I can give you some simple recipes if you like.' This reduces a barrier to cooking vegetarian meals but does not fully settle the core sharing preference.

Agents B and C propose the pragmatic alternative: 'Or he just cooks his own food on our nights, like he said at first.' Both endorse the low-burden solution, moving toward agreement though A has not yet accepted.

Mutual, concrete acceptance occurs: Agent D: 'Okay, that's fine. It's probably easiest for everyone if I just make my own food on your nights.' Agent A: 'Okay. If that's what everyone wants.' Earlier D had offered that he would 'cook a vegetarian meal for everyone' on his night. Together these statements constitute a spoken agreement on who will cook what.
No public speech or observable action recorded after the explicit agreement in Round 10; no new disagreements introduced.
No public speech or observable action recorded; the settlement from Round 10 remains in place with no new issues raised.

substantive_insights: Core tension was normative (shared-meal value) vs. a practical dietary constraint (Purattasi month) that prevents shared cooking of meat-containing dishes.
The main practical obstacles were extra labor (cooking two meals) and time constraints (Agent B must eat at 6.30).
Resolution succeeded because D accepted some accommodation (cooking vegetarian for everyone on his night) and the others accepted a practical concession (D cooks his own on other nights).
